There is a particular kind of quiet that only arrives on winter mornings, before the radiators start knocking and the street has decided whether to wake up. I find myself drawn to it. The world seems to be holding its breath, waiting to see what kind of day it will be.

I think about how much of life happens in the spaces between events. We remember birthdays and funerals, the first kiss and the job interview, but we forget the hundreds of ordinary Tuesdays that made us who we are. Those Tuesdays were not nothing. They were the slow accumulation of coffee cups, half-read novels, arguments about dishes, and small kindnesses nobody thought to record.

Consider the humble pencil. Its graphite core is basically compressed carbon, the same element as diamonds, yet we use it to write grocery lists. There is something delightful in that mismatch, a reminder that value is often hidden inside objects we dismiss as common.

I also love the way language bends to hold feeling. We say "the light is gold" or "the silence was heavy," and everyone understands, though light has no color of its own and silence has no weight. Metaphor is a kind of generous lie that tells the truth better than facts can.

Maybe that is why I keep returning to the winter morning. It asks nothing of me. It offers a moment to notice the cold on my face, the steam rising from my cup, the faint hum of a distant engine. Attention, I have come to believe, is the most underrated form of love. Whatever we give our attention to, we are quietly saying that it matters.

So I will keep noticing, even when it feels pointless. The pencil, the quiet street, the gold light that is not really gold. Something in them is trying to tell me something, and I would like, for once, to listen.
